extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principled criteria for forming and evaluating inductive generalizations, causal inferences, and natural classification across the sciences. Focuses on what counts as sufficient experience, the scope of uniformity, the role of abstraction, probability reasoning, and common fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of uniformity in generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations do not imply that there is uniformity in every thing, but only that as much uniformity as existed within the observation existed also beyond it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive statements (e.g., 'fire burns') do not require assuming that all nature obeys uniform laws — only that the observed class of phenomena exhibits uniformity which experience proves. Do not treat the induction as asserting universal pervasion beyond what experience supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causation is empirical, not a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of causation is not known a priori; it is itself a conclusion from experience rather than an antecedent assumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating causation as an intuition-based, self-evident principle independent of observation. The validity of causal laws rests on their verification by repeated experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction does not provide independent evidence of universal facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract conceptions elicited from experience cannot serve as evidence of objective facts in universal Nature beyond what the experience itself warrants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically assess claims that appeal to 'abstraction' as delivering assurance of universality; abstraction may clarify or analyze experience but does not extend empirical warrant beyond observed testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of high probability for practical action
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if not certain, a very high degree of probability justifies acting on a presumption until an exception appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical reliance requires probabilistic—not absolute—assurance. The keys-and-chambers example illustrates that lacking perfect certainty, strong probability still legitimizes action and expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing global uniformity from special causal sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: The uniformity of the course of nature as a whole is constituted by the uniform sequences of special effects from special natural agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the number and combinations of natural agencies relevant to the phenomena are sufficiently observed and amenable to enquiry; if so, the observed special sequences justify generalizing to wider uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles treated as invoking new antecedent causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged miracles are not exceptions to the law of causation but are cases where a new antecedent (the volition of a supernatural being) is affirmed to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating alleged miraculous events, analyze whether a purported new cause is being invoked rather than treating the event as a law-violating anomaly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive inference to the future justified like inferences about unobserved past
rubrics_metrics.description: Though we have not experienced the future, we have experienced what was once future; the presumption that the future will resemble the past is verified when future events become present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat predictions about the future as inductive in the same manner as inferences about unobserved past events; the logical proof comes from repeated verification over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of Kinds requires conjunctive properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A Kind is commonly identified not by a single property but by several properties together (e.g., color, brightness, form together identify a diamond's Kind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying, require a conjunction of characteristic properties to identify a natural Kind; single properties may be shared with other Kinds and therefore be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat allotropic forms as distinct Kinds (in this framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine assumes that allotropic (different structural forms of the same chemical substance) forms are so many different Kinds, in the sense used in the treatise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether different structural or allotropic forms are treated as separate Kinds in classification and argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Canons of Induction to chemical composition and other sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases of chemical composition are cases of causation; thus the Canons of Induction are applicable to chemistry, though special adaptations for particular sciences may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exempt particular sciences (e.g., chemistry) from general inductive rules. Use general inductive methods as the foundation and introduce domain-specific adaptations only where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canons for sciences seeking classes = rules of Natural Classification
rubrics_metrics.description: For sciences where the goal is discovery of Classes (Natural Classes), the appropriate canons are the principles and rules of Natural Classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the scientific aim is classification, employ explicit principles of natural classification (as opposed to canons aimed at causal discovery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited inference from approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: From premises like 'Most A are B' and 'Most A are C' we may with certainty infer only that some B are C; this is the utmost limit when degrees of approximation are undefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-reaching conclusions from approximate or partial generalizations; recognize the logical limits of what can be deduced without precise metrics of approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine probabilities by analyzing underlying causes, not naive frequency multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: The frequency of a coincidence depends on the frequency and efficacy of underlying causes; naive multiplicative counting can lead to fallacies when estimating how often conjunctions hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing probabilities for conjunctions (e.g., an item being both A and C and also B), analyze the independent and joint operation of causes rather than mechanically multiplying marginal frequencies. Use causal reasoning to derive correct joint frequencies (illustrated by the 11-in-12 example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions should capture the real, central attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer definitions that express the real attribute (e.g., define parallel lines by equidistance rather than 'in same plane and never meeting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose definitions and primitives that reflect the essential property intended, to avoid needing extraneous axioms and to align verbal definitions with conceptual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility should be judged against complete induction
rubrics_metrics.description: An impossibility is that the truth of which would conflict with a complete induction — i.e., with the most conclusive evidence we possess of universal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not label phenomena impossible merely from present ignorance; many alleged impossibilities have been overturned as knowledge advanced. Use the standard of what would contradict a complete induction when deciding impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate or false conceptions in explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying inappropriate geometrical or other conceptions (ones without prototypes in nature) leads to false explanations; sometimes there is not just an inappropriate but a wholly imaginary conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the conceptual framework used to explain phenomena has correspondent prototypes in the facts; avoid importing fanciful or unrelated conceptual notions into causal explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for fallacies of overgeneralization and mistaken qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies such as à dicto secundum quid ad dictum simpliciter, fallacia accidentis, and à dicto secundum quid ad dictum secundum alterum quid arise from wrongful shifts between qualified and unqualified statements (example: assuming 'strong drink must be a cause of strength').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to the scope of premises and avoid dropping necessary qualifications or illegitimately generalizing particular statements. Consult classical lists of fallacies when checking arguments.
